commentary.bottom_line: Three studies of patient-facing chatbots suggest that feedback-driven refinement may improve user ratings and engagement, but the one before-and-after measure of reach showed no change except in the Spanish-language version. No study compared feedback use against no feedback use in clinical AI, so the recommendation rests mainly on 20 framework and commentary endorsements.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=2113) reported that user ratings reached the 3.5/5 benchmark on all metrics except health awareness after iterative refinement. The trial appears to test the chatbot rather than the feedback process itself, which lowers directness. Two descriptive studies lack comparators, and one showed null reach results. These limitations support a rating of low certainty.

Stakeholders interviewed about machine-learning decision support named missing feedback loops as a barrier to integration. This shows the gap exists but does not show that closing it prevents harm. None of the tested studies measured errors, adverse events, or whether feedback caught unsafe outputs before they reached patients.

All three tests took place in real deployments of consumer chatbots for maternal, newborn, or general health use. In the United States study, postpartum reach moved from 64.1% to 62.8% (OR 0.95, 0.85-1.05) after content and outreach were revised based on feedback. Collecting feedback and changing content may not by itself increase use.

The trial enrolled older, rural, low-literacy, and non-English-speaking participants in China. In the United States study, the Spanish version raised newborn reach from 58% to 66.2% (OR 1.42) while the English results stayed flat. This suggests that feedback from language-minority users may yield gains that pooled measures would hide.

The endorsements come from voluntary frameworks and guidance. CHAI states that feedback should be solicited, considered, and used, and FUTURE-AI recommends qualitative methods. No endorsement listed here cites a statute or FDA or ONC requirement, so health systems would adopt the practice as good governance rather than as a legal obligation.

In the India deployment, 64% of 110 mothers engaged with a nurse through the chatbot. Feedback-responsive designs may therefore generate human follow-up work that requires staffing. None of the studies reported the cost or staff time needed to collect, review, and act on feedback.

In the India study, 80% of users replied at least once and 64% reached a nurse. This suggests that patients will use a feedback channel when a human responds. The studies did not report whether patients saw their feedback change the tool, which affects trust.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized or compared deployments that acted on feedback against deployments that did not, and none addressed clinician-facing or diagnostic AI. The studies also did not measure safety outcomes, the time from feedback to correction, or staffing cost.
commentary.underserved_note: The trial included limited English proficiency, low health literacy, rural, minority, and older adult participants, and the United States study included Spanish-speaking and minority recipients. No study reported Medicaid or safety-net enrollment, so applying these findings to those settings remains an inference.
